Waterspouts
WAW-tur-spowts
n. pl. (cataracts or torrents of falling water; the noise under which the psalmist is overwhelmed)
A compound of water and spout, from Middle Dutch spuiten, to gush. It renders Hebrew tsinnor, a pipe, conduit or waterfall — used elsewhere of the gutter by which Joab entered Jerusalem.

Biblical Definition

Deep calleth unto deep at the noise of thy waterspouts: all thy waves and thy billows are gone over me. The psalmist is in exile from the sanctuary, cast down and disquieted, remembering God from the land of Jordan and the Hermonites — the headwaters, where the snowmelt comes off the mountain in cataracts. He hears the roar of falling water and hears his own life in it: one depth calling to another, wave after wave, nothing between them. Two things in the verse are easy to miss. The first is the possessive: thy waterspouts, thy waves, thy billows. He does not describe his troubles as accidents or as the work of enemies but as God's own water going over him. The second is the refrain that frames it on both sides — Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him. The man is preaching to himself in the middle of the noise, and the sermon is a command and a future tense. Jonah, in the belly of the fish, uses almost the same words: thou hadst cast me into the deep, all thy billows and thy waves passed over me. Both men knew whose water it was, and both were heard.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): a spout or gush of water; in the older sense, a cataract or fall of water from on high.

expand to see more

WATERSPOUT, n. A remarkable meteor, consisting of a cloud in the form of a cone, from which a column of water descends.

SPOUT, n. A pipe or a projecting mouth of a vessel, useful in directing the stream of a liquid.

BILLOW, n. A great wave or surge of the sea, occasioned usually by violent wind.

CATARACT, n. A great fall of water over a precipice.

DISQUIET, v.t. To disturb; to deprive of peace, rest or tranquillity; to make uneasy or restless.

Key Scripture

Psalm 42:7 — "Deep calleth unto deep at the noise of thy waterspouts: all thy waves and thy billows are gone over me."

Psalm 42:6 — "O my God, my soul is cast down within me: therefore will I remember thee from the land of Jordan, and of the Hermonites, from the hill Mizar."

Psalm 42:5 — "Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him for the help of his countenance."

Jonah 2:3 — "For thou hadst cast me into the deep, in the midst of the seas; and the floods compassed me about: all thy billows and thy waves passed over me."

Modern Corruption

Spiritual darkness is handled as a chemical problem or as a failure of faith; Psalm 42 gives a believer overwhelmed, naming the water as God's, and preaching to his own soul in the middle of it.

expand to see more

Two bad counsels meet over a man in Psalm 42's condition. The first treats the darkness as purely a defect of body or brain, a matter to be managed and nothing more; the second treats it as proof of unbelief, to be repented of. Scripture does neither. It gives the sufferer words — a whole psalm of them — and lets him say that his tears have been his meat day and night, that his soul is cast down, that deep calls to deep. It does not hurry him. Elijah under the juniper tree was given sleep and food before he was given a word, and the word, when it came, was not a rebuke.

But the psalm does not leave him lying there either. Three times it turns and addresses the man himself: Why art thou cast down, O my soul?... hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him. That is a believer taking himself in hand, arguing with his own feelings from what he knows, and refusing to let the loudest voice in the room be the water. The cure is not a mood he manufactures; it is a hope fixed on someone outside him, stated in the future tense — I shall yet praise him — and held while the billows are still going over.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tsinnor (H6794), a conduit or waterfall; tehom (H8415), the deep; mishbar (H4867), a breaker or wave; gal (H1530), a billow.

expand to see more

Hebrew tsinnor (H6794) — a pipe or cataract; used only here and of the gutter at the taking of Jerusalem.

Hebrew tehom (H8415) — the deep; the same word as the deep upon whose face darkness lay in Genesis 1.

Hebrew mishbar (H4867) — a breaker; rendered waves, and used again by Jonah.

Hebrew gal (H1530) — a billow, a heap; the second of the two words rolling over the psalmist.

Hebrew yachal (H3176) — to wait, to hope; the command the psalmist gives his own soul.

Usage

"“Deep calleth unto deep at the noise of thy waterspouts” — trouble heard as one wave summoning the next."

"“all thy waves and thy billows” — the possessive that changes the whole psalm."

"“hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him” — a man preaching to himself."
